author: blaise-pascal
fields.title: Pensées (For Teens)
fields.description: Blaise Pascal invented a calculating machine at nineteen, helped found the mathematics of chance, and then, one night in 1654, met God. He spent his last years writing notes for a book defending the Christian faith, and died before he could finish it. Those notes, the Pensées (“thoughts”), are still read everywhere. This teen edition retells his biggest ideas in plain words: why we can’t sit still, why we are always getting ready to live, the thinking reed, the heart’s reasons, the famous wager, and the God who is found by those who seek him. Pascal’s own sentences are kept where they say it best.
fields.hook: A teenage genius's big questions about boredom, happiness, doubt and God, in plain words.

qa.question: Who was Blaise Pascal?
qa.answer: A French mathematician, scientist and Christian thinker, born in 1623 in Clermont. As a teenager he wrote on geometry and built a calculating machine; his experiments showed that the air has weight, and his letters with Fermat founded the mathematics of probability. After meeting God on the night of 23 November 1654, he gave his gifts to defending the Christian faith. He died in Paris in 1662, aged thirty-nine.

qa.question: What does “Pensées” mean?
qa.answer: It is French for “thoughts”. Pascal was gathering notes for a big book defending Christianity, but illness stopped him finishing it. After his death his friends published the notes, some long and some only a line, under that title.

qa.question: What is Pascal’s wager?
qa.answer: Pascal’s argument that everyone has to bet their life either that God is or that he is not, because not choosing is also a choice. If you bet on God and are right, you gain everything; if you are wrong, you lose very little. Pascal did not think the wager could make anyone believe. He used it to wake people up, and then pointed them to seek God honestly.

qa.question: What did Pascal mean by “The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know”?
qa.answer: Not that feelings beat facts. Pascal loved reason and used it brilliantly. He meant that we know some of the deepest things, including God, not only by working them out but by a knowing deeper than argument, which he called the heart. Faith uses both.

qa.question: Pascal says a lot about human misery. Is this book depressing?
qa.answer: No. Pascal is honest about how restless and messed up people are, but only so that we will see how great we are too, and how much we need Jesus. He says knowing our misery without God leads to despair, and knowing God without our misery leads to pride; Jesus shows us both and heals us. If you are feeling low most days, please talk to a trusted adult.

qa.question: Was Pascal Catholic or Protestant?
qa.answer: He was a Roman Catholic, close to a strict renewal group centred on the convent of Port-Royal near Paris. Christians of every tradition have read and loved the Pensées, and this retelling keeps to the parts all of them share.

qa.question: Is this the full text?
qa.answer: No. It is a retelling for teenagers in plain modern words, drawn from across the Pensées and keeping Pascal’s own sentences where they say it best. The full Pensées is also available.

fields.title: The Genius Who Met Fire
fields.body_html:
“I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” — Exodus 3:6 (KJV)

Imagine a boy who teaches himself geometry before anyone gets round to teaching him. Blaise Pascal was born in 1623 in Clermont, in central France. His mother died when he was small, and his father, a clever and careful man, taught him at home in Paris.

At sixteen Blaise wrote a treatise on geometry that impressed the leading mathematicians of the day. At nineteen he built a calculating machine to help his father with the endless sums of his job as a tax official. Later his experiments on a mountain called the Puy de Dôme showed that the air has weight, and his letters with another mathematician, Fermat, helped found the mathematics of chance and probability. Scientists still measure pressure in a unit named after him: the pascal.

But his life was not easy. From the age of eighteen, he said, he never passed a day without pain. His body was weak, and he was often ill.

In 1646, when Pascal was in his early twenties, his family met some very devout Christians linked to a convent called Port-Royal, near Paris, and they were all stirred up about God. But for Blaise the change did not yet go deep. For a while he was more interested in his work, his friends and his reputation.

Then, on the night of 23 November 1654, alone in his room, something happened that changed him for good. He met God. Afterwards he wrote down what he had experienced on a scrap of paper and sewed it into the lining of his coat, and he kept it with him for the rest of his life. It begins like this:

“FIRE. God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and the learned. Certainty, certainty, feeling, joy, peace. God of Jesus Christ.”

Notice what he says. Pascal was one of the cleverest people alive. He knew all the arguments about God. But that night he met not an idea, a God “of the philosophers and the learned”, but the living God who had spoken to real people like Abraham and who had come to us in Jesus Christ. And what he felt was not confusion but certainty, joy and peace.

Pascal spent the rest of his short life using his brilliant mind for that God. He began a great book to help people who doubted or did not care about Christianity. Illness stopped him finishing it. When he died, his friends found piles of notes, some pages long, some only one line. They published them as the Pensées, which is French for “thoughts”.

This book retells the best of those thoughts. They are about things you know very well: boredom, phones and distraction, wanting people to like you, feeling tiny in a huge universe, doubts, and whether God is real. Pascal wrote them nearly four hundred years ago, but they could have been written about you.

One thing to do this week: keep a “thoughts” notebook this week, on paper or on your phone. Each day write one honest question you have about God, life or yourself. Don’t try to answer them yet. Just notice what your real questions are.

study_questions.question: What did Pascal achieve as a young man?
study_questions.answer: He wrote a treatise on geometry at sixteen, built a calculating machine at nineteen, showed that the air has weight, and helped found the mathematics of probability.

study_questions.question: What happened on the night of 23 November 1654?
study_questions.answer: Alone in his room, Pascal met God. He wrote down the experience and sewed it into his coat, keeping it for the rest of his life.

study_questions.question: What is the difference between the God of the philosophers and the God of Abraham?
study_questions.answer: A God “of the philosophers and the learned” is an idea people argue about; the God of Abraham is the living God who speaks to real people and is known personally through Jesus Christ.

fields.title: Why We Can’t Sit Still
fields.body_html:
“Be still, and know that I am God.” — Psalm 46:10 (KJV)

Try this. Sit in a room with no phone, no music, no book and nobody to talk to, and do nothing for ten minutes. Most people find it surprisingly hard. After a minute or two you start to fidget. Your hand reaches for your pocket.

Pascal noticed this long before anyone had a phone. He looked at all the things people do, wars, games, parties, careers, risky adventures, and came to a startling conclusion:

“I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.”

Why can’t we? Pascal says that when we are completely still, with nothing to distract us, we start to think about our lives: that we are weak, that we will one day die, that we are not in control. And that feels unbearable. So we fill every gap with noise.

“Nothing is so insufferable to man as to be completely at rest, without passions, without business, without diversion, without study. He then feels his nothingness, his forlornness, his insufficiency, his dependence, his weakness, his emptiness.”

Pascal’s word for all the things we use to avoid thinking is “diversion”. In his day it meant hunting, card games, dancing and court gossip. In ours it might mean endless scrolling, gaming, streaming one more episode, or having something playing in our ears every waking moment.

He makes a funny point about hunting. A man will spend a whole day chasing a hare that he would not even want if you offered it to him as a gift. It is not the hare he wants; it is the chase. We like the chase better than the catch, because the chase keeps us from thinking. Pascal even says that kings, who have everything, need people around them all day whose only job is to keep them amused, because a king who has time to think about himself is unhappy.

Pascal is not saying games or films are wicked. He is asking an honest question: why do I need them so much? What am I running from?

His answer is that there is an emptiness in us that we are trying not to feel. Distraction does not fill it. It only stops us noticing it for a while. The Bible’s answer is not more noise but a different kind of stillness: “Be still, and know that I am God.” Being still before God is not empty. It is where the emptiness can actually start to be filled.

If the quiet makes you feel more than just bored, if sadness or worry floods in whenever things go still and won’t lift, that matters. Please talk to a parent, a youth leader, a school counsellor or a doctor. You don’t have to handle it alone.

One thing to do this week: once a day this week, spend five minutes with no phone or screen nearby. Sit still, read one verse of a psalm, and tell God honestly what comes into your mind. Notice how it feels at the start of the week and at the end.

study_questions.question: According to Pascal, where does all the unhappiness of men come from?
study_questions.answer: From the fact that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal mean by “diversion”?
study_questions.answer: All the activities we use to stop ourselves thinking about our real condition, our weakness, our death and our need.

study_questions.question: Why does the hunter prefer the chase to the hare?
study_questions.answer: Because it is the busyness of the chase, not the hare itself, that keeps him from thinking about his life.

fields.title: Always Getting Ready to Live
fields.body_html:
“Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” — Matthew 6:34 (KJV)

Have you ever thought, “I’ll be happy when…”? When the exams are over. When I’m sixteen. When I’ve got that phone. When I’m out of school. When I’m in a relationship. When the holidays come.

Pascal noticed that we are almost never living in the present moment. We are either replaying the past or planning the future.

“The present is never our end. The past and the present are our means; the future alone is our end. So we never live, but we hope to live; and, as we are always preparing to be happy, it is inevitable we should never be so.”

That is a sharp observation. If happiness is always “when”, it never actually arrives, because as soon as you get there, there is a new “when”. You finish the exams and start worrying about results. You get the phone and want the next one.

Pascal says that experience keeps fooling us. Something doesn’t satisfy us, so we think the next thing will. It doesn’t, so we try again, always hoping that this time will be different. He describes it like this: experience dupes us, and from misfortune to misfortune leads us to death.

Jesus spoke into exactly this restlessness. He told his followers not to be anxious about tomorrow, because tomorrow will take care of itself. That is not an instruction to stop planning or to give up on your future. It is an invitation to stop living somewhere else, in your worries or your daydreams, and to live today, with God, here.

This matters because God is not in the “when”. He is in the now. You will never meet him in a future that hasn’t happened yet or a past you can’t change. You meet him in this moment, this conversation, this task, this walk home.

Pascal also notices how much we dodge the present when it is uncomfortable. If now is painful or dull, we jump ahead in our minds to somewhere nicer. But that means we never deal with what is actually in front of us, and we never discover that God is with us in it.

None of this means your hopes and plans are wrong. It means they can’t carry the weight of your happiness. Only God can do that, and he is here today.

One thing to do this week: each evening this week, write down one good thing that happened today, not tomorrow or yesterday, and thank God for it. When you catch yourself thinking “I’ll be happy when…”, pause and say, “Lord, you are here now.”

study_questions.question: What does Pascal mean by “we never live, but we hope to live”?
study_questions.answer: We are always focused on the future, getting ready to be happy, so we never actually live and enjoy the present.

study_questions.question: Why does happiness that is always “when” never arrive?
study_questions.answer: Because as soon as we reach one goal, we set the next one, and the present is never enough for us.

study_questions.question: What does Jesus say about tomorrow in Matthew 6:34?
study_questions.answer: Not to be anxious about it, because tomorrow will take care of itself; each day has enough of its own trouble.

fields.title: Wanting Fans
fields.body_html:
“How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only?” — John 5:44 (KJV)

Pascal had a sharp eye for one particular weakness: our need to be admired.

“Vanity is so anchored in the heart of man that a soldier, a soldier’s servant, a cook, a porter brags, and wishes to have his admirers.”

Then he turns it round on himself. Even philosophers want admirers, he says. People who write against vanity want the glory of having written well, and people who read them want the glory of having read them. “I who write this have perhaps this desire,” he admits, “and perhaps those who will read it ...” He leaves the sentence hanging. He is talking about you and me.

If Pascal were alive today he would have plenty to say about likes, followers, views and streaks. But he had already noticed something strange about the way we want approval:

“We are so presumptuous that we would wish to be known by all the world, even by people who shall come after, when we shall be no more; and we are so vain that the esteem of five or six neighbours delights and contents us.”

Both halves are true. We dream of being famous, and yet a few people saying something nice about us can make our whole day. And a few people ignoring us or saying something unkind can wreck it.

Pascal also saw where this starts. He wrote that admiration spoils everything from childhood: “Ah! How well said! Ah! How well done! How well-behaved he is!” From the time we are small, we learn to perform for praise. That isn’t because the adults around us are bad. It is how human hearts work.

The trouble is that living for other people’s approval is exhausting. You are never sure you have enough. You keep checking. You shape what you say and wear and post around what will get a good reaction. And you can find yourself saying things you don’t believe just to fit in.

Jesus asked a pointed question: how can you believe, if you are always looking for honour from each other instead of from God? Faith gets crowded out when people’s opinion matters more to us than God’s.

The way out is not to stop caring about people. It is to settle where your real worth comes from. God made you, knows you completely and loves you in Christ. You do not have to earn that by performing. When that sinks in, other people’s approval becomes a nice extra rather than the air you breathe.

One thing to do this week: notice this week every time you do something mainly to be seen or liked: a post, a joke, a comment, an outfit. Don’t beat yourself up. Just say quietly, “Lord, your opinion of me is the one that counts.” Try doing one kind thing that nobody will know about.

study_questions.question: Who does Pascal say wants admirers?
study_questions.answer: Everyone, from soldiers, cooks and porters to philosophers, writers and readers, including Pascal himself.

study_questions.question: What two opposite things does Pascal notice about our wish to be admired?
study_questions.answer: We want to be known by the whole world, even after we die, and yet the good opinion of five or six neighbours is enough to delight us.

study_questions.question: How does Jesus say seeking honour from people affects faith?
study_questions.answer: It makes it hard to believe, because we are looking for honour from each other rather than from God.

fields.title: The Thinking Reed
fields.body_html:
“I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.” — Psalm 139:14 (KJV)

Look up at the night sky on a clear night, away from street lights, and you can feel very small. Pascal felt that too. One of his most famous lines is just a single sentence:

“The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me.”

He describes how tiny a person is in the whole of nature. The earth is a point next to the path of the sun, and that is a fine point compared with the stars. And then he turns the other way, into the very small, and finds endless worlds there too. We are caught in the middle. He asks:

“For in fact what is man in nature? A Nothing in comparison with the Infinite, an All in comparison with the Nothing, a mean between nothing and everything.”

So are we just specks of dust? Pascal says no, and gives one of the most beautiful pictures in the whole book:

“Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed. The entire universe need not arm itself to crush him. A vapour, a drop of water suffices to kill him. But, if the universe were to crush him, man would still be more noble than that which killed him, because he knows that he dies and the advantage which the universe has over him; the universe knows nothing of this.”

Think about that. A reed is a thin plant by a river that bends in every wind. That is how fragile we are. A virus, an accident or a fall can kill us. But the universe, with all its stars and galaxies, cannot think. It does not know it exists. You do. You can wonder, love, pray, ask questions, and know that you will die. That makes you greater than all the stars.

Pascal concludes: “All our dignity consists, then, in thought.” And then he adds a simple instruction: “Let us endeavour, then, to think well.”

The Bible says something similar, but goes further. In Psalm 8 David looks at the moon and stars and asks what man is, that God should care about him. And Psalm 139 says we are fearfully and wonderfully made. Our greatness is not only that we can think. It is that the God who made the stars made us to know him.

So when you feel small, you are right: you are. But you are not unimportant. A thinking reed, made in the image of God, matters more to him than every galaxy.

One thing to do this week: go outside one evening this week and look at the sky. Say Psalm 8:3–4 to God: “When I consider thy heavens… what is man, that thou art mindful of him?” Then thank him that he made you able to think about him.

study_questions.question: Why does Pascal call man a “reed”?
study_questions.answer: Because we are fragile, the feeblest thing in nature, easily killed by a vapour or a drop of water.

study_questions.question: Why is a thinking reed greater than the whole universe?
study_questions.answer: Because a person knows that they die and knows the universe’s power over them, while the universe knows nothing at all.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal tell us to do with our ability to think?
study_questions.answer: “Let us endeavour, then, to think well.”

A reed is a thin plant by a river that bends in every wind. That is how fragile we are. A virus, an accident or a fall can kill us. But the universe, with all its stars and galaxies, cannot think. It does not know it exists. You do. You can wonder, love, pray, ask questions, and know that you will die. That makes you greater than all the stars. Pascal concludes: “All our dignity consists, then, in thought.” And then he adds a simple instruction: “Let us endeavour, then, to think well.” The Bible says something similar, but goes further. In Psalm 8 David looks at the moon and stars and asks what man is, that God should care about him. And Psalm 139 says we are fearfully and wonderfully made. Our greatness is not only that we can think. It is that the God who made the stars made us to know him. So when you feel small, you are right: you are. But you are not unimportant. A thinking reed, made in the image of God, matters more to him than every galaxy. One thing to do this week: go outside one evening this week and look at the sky. Say Psalm 8:3–4 to God: “When I consider thy heavens… what is man, that thou art mindful of him?” Then thank him that he made you able to think about him.

fields.title: Great and Messed Up
fields.body_html:
“Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.” — Ecclesiastes 7:29 (KJV)

Pascal could not stop being amazed at how strange human beings are. We are capable of brilliant science and terrible cruelty, deep love and petty spite, all in the same person, sometimes on the same day.

“What a chimera then is man! What a novelty! What a monster, what a chaos, what a contradiction, what a prodigy! Judge of all things, imbecile worm of the earth; depositary of truth, a sink of uncertainty and error; the pride and refuse of the universe!”

A chimera was a creature from old stories made of different animals stuck together. Pascal says that is what we are like: a mix that doesn’t make sense. We are great and we are wretched.

But even our misery, he says, shows our greatness. A tree does not know it is miserable. A ruined house is not sad. Only people feel that something is wrong.

“The greatness of man is great in that he knows himself to be miserable.”

Pascal says our miseries are the miseries of “a great lord”, “a deposed king”. A king who has lost his throne is only sad because he remembers he was once a king. We feel that we were made for something better because we were.

So where does the mix come from? Philosophers in Pascal’s time either said humans are wonderful or said they are hopeless. Pascal says both are half right. Only the Bible explains both halves together. God made us good and great, in his image. But we turned away from him, and now we are broken. We still carry traces of the greatness, like the ruins of a beautiful building.

He puts it in one of his sharpest questions: “If man is not made for God, why is he only happy in God? If man is made for God, why is he so opposed to God?” The answer is that we were made for God and fell away from him.

Pascal also warns against two mistakes. One is to think you are great and forget you are fallen. That leads to pride. The other is to think you are only rubbish. That leads to despair. Both are lies. He says plainly that a person should love themselves, “for there is in him a nature capable of good”, but not love the evil that is in them too.

If you tend to think the worst of yourself, hear this: being honest that you are a sinner is not the same as hating yourself. God made you, and he wants to heal you, not crush you. And if negative thoughts about yourself feel constant or heavy, tell someone you trust.

One thing to do this week: this week, write two lists: three ways you can see God’s image in you (gifts, kindness, creativity) and three ways you know you need his help. Pray over both lists, thanking him for the first and asking his help with the second.

study_questions.question: What is a chimera, and why does Pascal compare people to one?
study_questions.answer: A creature made of different animals put together; people are a puzzling mix of greatness and wretchedness.

study_questions.question: How does our misery prove our greatness?
study_questions.answer: Only a great being can know it is miserable; like a deposed king, we feel the loss because we were made for something better.

study_questions.question: What two mistakes does Pascal warn against?
study_questions.answer: Thinking we are only great, which leads to pride, and thinking we are only wretched, which leads to despair.

fields.title: The Hole Only God Can Fill
fields.body_html:
“As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.” — Psalm 42:1–2 (KJV)

Pascal begins this part of his thinking with a simple fact:

“All men seek happiness. This is without exception.”

Everything anyone does, he says, is aimed at being happy. One person goes to war and another avoids it, but both are trying to be happy. The will never takes the least step except towards that goal.

And yet, Pascal says, nobody ever seems to get there. Rich and poor, young and old, famous and unknown, all of them complain. Everybody wants something they haven’t got.

Why? Pascal’s answer is one of the most famous ideas in the book. He says that this desire, and our failure to satisfy it, are a clue. They show that there was once a true happiness in us, and that only its “mark and empty trace” is left. We try to fill that empty space with everything around us, and nothing works.

“But these are all inadequate, because the infinite abyss can only be filled by an infinite and immutable object, that is to say, only by God Himself.”

People often sum this up by saying we have a “God-shaped hole” inside us. Pascal’s own words are stronger: an infinite abyss. Something infinite can only be filled by Someone infinite.

Pascal adds a list that is almost funny. Since we have turned away from God, he says, people have tried to put almost anything in his place: the stars, the heavens, the earth, plants, cabbages, leeks, animals, insects. Today we might add money, grades, sport, music, relationships, looks, followers. None of them are bad. But none of them are God, and if we make any of them our ultimate happiness, it will eventually let us down.

This explains a lot about life. It is why the thing you wanted so badly feels flat once you have it. It is why even good things, like friendship, cannot carry the weight of everything. It is why people who seem to have it all can still be unhappy.

The psalm at the top of this chapter is a prayer from someone who has noticed this thirst and knows where it points: “My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God.” The thirst is not a problem to be ignored or numbed. It is a signpost. It is God calling you to come back home.

One thing to do this week: think about the thing you most often turn to when you feel empty or bored. This week, each time you reach for it, pause first and pray: “Lord, you are the one I am really thirsty for.” Then carry on, if it is something good, but with your heart turned to God.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal say every person is seeking?
study_questions.answer: Happiness, without exception; every action is aimed at it.

study_questions.question: Why can’t anything in the world fill the “infinite abyss” in us?
study_questions.answer: Because only something infinite and unchanging, God himself, can fill it.

study_questions.question: What things does Pascal say people put in God’s place?
study_questions.answer: Almost anything: the stars, the heavens, the earth, plants, cabbages, leeks, animals, insects.

fields.title: The Heart Has Its Reasons
fields.body_html:
“Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind.” — Matthew 22:37 (KJV)

Pascal was a scientist and mathematician. He loved proof. So it may surprise you that his most famous single sentence is about something reason can’t do:

“The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.”

People sometimes take this to mean that feelings matter more than facts, or that you should believe whatever you want. That is not what Pascal meant at all.

By “the heart” he did not mean emotions. He meant the deepest part of us, where we know things directly, without working them out step by step. He gives an example. You know that you are awake and not dreaming. You cannot prove it with an argument, but you know it. In the same way, he says, we know first principles, like the fact that there is space and time and number, by the heart, not by reason. Reason builds on them.

“We know truth, not only by the reason, but also by the heart.”

And then he applies this to God: “It is the heart which experiences God, and not the reason. This, then, is faith: God felt by the heart, not by the reason.” Faith, he says, is a gift from God.

But Pascal does not throw away reason. He loved it too much. He says there are two mistakes: “to exclude reason, to admit reason only.” Christianity is not against thinking. You should ask hard questions, study the evidence, and use your mind. Jesus said to love God with all your mind as well as your heart.

Pascal also says that reason is at its best when it recognises its own limits:

“The last proceeding of reason is to recognise that there is an infinity of things which are beyond it.”

This is a good reminder for anyone who thinks science has made God unnecessary. Science is wonderful, and Pascal was a great scientist. But science cannot tell you whether your life has meaning, why there is something rather than nothing, or whether God loves you. Those questions are real, and reason alone cannot finish answering them.

So when you have doubts, think them through. Read, ask, discuss. But also pay attention to the deeper knowing of the heart: the longing for God, the sense that life is more than chance, the way Jesus’ words ring true. God speaks to the whole of you.

One thing to do this week: write down one question about God or faith that bugs you. This week, find one thing to read or one wise Christian to ask about it, and also bring the question to God in prayer. Use both your mind and your heart.

study_questions.question: What did Pascal mean by “the heart”?
study_questions.answer: Not just emotions, but the deepest part of us that knows things directly, like the fact that we are awake, without proving them by argument.

study_questions.question: What two extremes does Pascal warn against?
study_questions.answer: Excluding reason, and admitting only reason.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal say is “the last proceeding of reason”?
study_questions.answer: To recognise that there are infinitely many things beyond it.

fields.title: The Wager
fields.body_html:
“Choose you this day whom ye will serve.” — Joshua 24:15 (KJV)

Pascal’s most famous argument uses the mathematics of chance he helped invent. It has become known as Pascal’s wager.

He imagines talking to someone who says, “I can’t tell whether God exists. Reason can’t decide. So I won’t choose at all.” Pascal replies:

“Yes; but you must wager. It is not optional. You are embarked.”

“Embarked” means you are already on the boat. You are already alive, already living one way or another. Not deciding is itself a decision, because you are living as though God does not matter.

So Pascal says, let’s think about it like a bet. If you bet that God exists and you are right, you gain everything: eternal life and happiness. If you bet that God exists and you are wrong, what have you lost? Some pleasures, maybe. Then he says:

“Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is. Let us estimate these two chances. If you gain, you gain all; if you lose, you lose nothing. Wager, then, without hesitation that He is.”

His opponent replies, in effect: “Fine, but I can’t just make myself believe.” Pascal agrees. The wager can’t make you believe. Its job is to show you that the question matters enormously and that seeking God is worth it. Then he gives practical advice: look at people who have come to faith and follow the way they began, by acting as if they believed. In Pascal’s Catholic church, that meant things like taking holy water and attending Mass. For you it might mean praying, reading the Bible, going to church, and spending time with people who follow Jesus.

Then he says what you would actually lose by living for God:

“You will be faithful, honest, humble, grateful, generous, a sincere friend, truthful.”

You would not have certain “poisonous pleasures”, like glory and luxury. But Pascal promises that every step you take on this road, you will see more of what you have gained and how little you gave up.

Some people think the wager is a cold, selfish argument: believe in God just in case. But remember who Pascal was. He had met God in fire. The wager is not where faith ends. It is a wake-up call for people who are drifting, to get them to start seeking. And Pascal is honest that the stakes are real. Elsewhere he says he would be far more afraid of being mistaken and then finding that the Christian religion was true, than of believing it and not being mistaken.

One thing to do this week: if you have been drifting, “not deciding” about God, make a decision to seek him seriously for one month. Start this week: pray every day, even if it is only “God, if you’re there, show me”, and read one chapter of Mark’s Gospel each day.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal mean by “You are embarked”?
study_questions.answer: We are already in the boat of life; not choosing is itself a choice, so everyone has to wager.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal say you gain and lose if you wager that God exists?
study_questions.answer: If you win, you gain everything; if you lose, you lose nothing.

study_questions.question: What practical advice does Pascal give to someone who wants to believe but can’t?
study_questions.answer: To follow the way others began, by acting as if they believed and taking part in the practices of faith.

fields.title: Seekers
fields.body_html:
“And ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.” — Jeremiah 29:13 (KJV)

Pascal divided people into three groups:

“There are only three kinds of persons; those who serve God, having found Him; others who are occupied in seeking Him, not having found Him; while the remainder live without seeking Him, and without having found Him. The first are reasonable and happy, the last are foolish and unhappy; those between are unhappy and reasonable.”

Notice how kind he is to seekers. People who are honestly looking for God but have not found him yet are, he says, reasonable. They are on the right track. It is uncomfortable, but it is not foolish. What is foolish, he says, is not to look at all, to go through life never asking the biggest question there is.

Pascal said something similar about how he judged others. He did not approve of those who simply praised humanity, or those who simply criticised it, or those who just amused themselves. He said, “I can only approve of those who seek with lamentation”: people who take the question seriously enough to feel it.

Why doesn’t God just make himself obvious? Pascal had thought about this a lot. He says the Bible itself talks about a hidden God. God has given enough signs to be found by those who really want to find him, but not so many that people are forced to believe against their will.

“There is enough light for those who only desire to see, and enough obscurity for those who have a contrary disposition.”

That means the question is not only “Is there enough evidence?” but also “Do I want God to be there?” Some people, if they are honest, don’t want God, because he would change things. Pascal invites us to be honest about that too.

There is a great promise for seekers in the Bible. God says through the prophet Jeremiah: you will seek me and find me, when you search for me with all your heart. Jesus said, “Seek, and ye shall find.”

If you are a seeker right now, unsure, asking questions, not quite there, take heart. You are not a failure as a Christian or a bad person for having questions. You are exactly where Pascal says a reasonable person should be. Keep seeking, with your whole heart. God is not hiding to tease you. He wants to be found.

And if you already know God, remember to be patient with seekers. They are on a journey, and God is at work in it.

One thing to do this week: ask yourself honestly this week which of Pascal’s three groups you are in. Write it down. Then pray Jeremiah 29:13 back to God: “Lord, I want to seek you with all my heart. Let me find you.”

study_questions.question: What are Pascal’s three kinds of people?
study_questions.answer: Those who serve God having found him; those who seek him but haven’t found him; and those who neither seek nor find.

study_questions.question: Why does Pascal call seekers “reasonable”?
study_questions.answer: Because they are taking the most important question seriously and looking for God, even though they haven’t found him yet.

study_questions.question: Why, according to Pascal, doesn’t God make himself completely obvious?
study_questions.answer: He gives enough light for those who want to see, and enough obscurity for those who don’t, so that people are not forced against their will.

fields.title: What We Say to Ourselves
fields.body_html:
“Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.” — Philippians 4:8 (KJV)

Pascal noticed something about the voice in our heads long before anyone talked about “self-talk”:

“Man is so made that by continually telling him he is a fool he believes it, and by continually telling it to himself he makes himself believe it. For man holds an inward talk with his self alone, which it behoves him to regulate well.”

Think about the things you say to yourself in a day. “I’m so stupid.” “Nobody likes me.” “I always mess things up.” “I’ll never be good enough.” Pascal says that what you keep repeating, you end up believing.

So, he says, we need to “regulate” our inward talk. That means paying attention to it and choosing what we feed it. His advice is to talk to ourselves of God, “whom we know to be true”, and so convince ourselves of the truth.

This is not the same as just thinking positive thoughts. It is about telling yourself what is true. If you have done something wrong, it is true that you have sinned, and it is also true that Jesus forgives. If you feel worthless, it is true that you are made in God’s image and loved by him. The Bible gives us words to say to ourselves when our own words are cruel or false.

Pascal also saw something humbling about how we take criticism. He said we owe a great debt to those who point out our faults. It hurts, but it helps us grow. A true friend who tells you something hard is giving you a gift.

But notice the balance. Listening to honest, loving correction is different from soaking up constant put-downs from people who want to make you small. If someone keeps telling you that you are stupid or worthless, that is not correction. It is harm, and you should tell a trusted adult. And if the voice in your own head is relentlessly harsh and won’t stop, that is worth telling someone too. It is not a weakness to need help.

Paul’s words at the top of this chapter give us a filter for our thoughts: true, honest, just, pure, lovely, of good report. Run your inner talk through that filter. Is what you are saying to yourself true? Is it the way God talks about you?

One thing to do this week: write down three things you often say to yourself in your head. For each, ask: is this true? Is this how God sees me? Then write a true sentence to replace any that are false, and say it to yourself each morning.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal say happens when we keep telling ourselves something?
study_questions.answer: We end up believing it; our inner talk shapes what we think is true.

study_questions.question: What does Pascal advise us to talk to ourselves about?
study_questions.answer: About God, whom we know to be true, so that we convince ourselves of the truth.

study_questions.question: How is honest correction different from constant put-downs?
study_questions.answer: Loving correction helps us grow and is a gift; constant put-downs meant to make us small are harmful and should be told to a trusted adult.

fields.body_text: “Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.” — Philippians 4:8 (KJV) Pascal noticed something about the voice in our heads long before anyone talked about “self-talk”: “Man is so made that by continually telling him he is a fool he believes it, and by continually telling it to himself he makes himself believe it. For man holds an inward talk with his self alone, which it behoves him to regulate well.” Think about the things you say to yourself in a day. “I’m so stupid.” “Nobody likes me.” “I always mess things up.” “I’ll never be good enough.” Pascal says that what you keep repeating, you end up believing. So, he says, we need to “regulate” our inward talk. That means paying attention to it and choosing what we feed it. His advice is to talk to ourselves of God, “whom we know to be true”, and so convince ourselves of the truth. This is not the same as just thinking positive thoughts. It is about telling yourself what is true. If you have done something wrong, it is true that you have sinned, and it is also true that Jesus forgives. If you feel worthless, it is true that you are made in God’s image and loved by him. The Bible gives us words to say to ourselves when our own words are cruel or false. Pascal also saw something humbling about how we take criticism. He said we owe a great debt to those who point out our faults. It hurts, but it helps us grow. A true friend who tells you something hard is giving you a gift. But notice the balance. Listening to honest, loving correction is different from soaking up constant put-downs from people who want to make you small. If someone keeps telling you that you are stupid or worthless, that is not correction. It is harm, and you should tell a trusted adult. And if the voice in your own head is relentlessly harsh and won’t stop, that is worth telling someone too. It is not a weakness to need help. Is this how God sees me? Then write a true sentence to replace any that are false, and say it to yourself each morning.

fields.title: Knowing God Through Jesus
fields.body_html:
“Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6 (KJV)

After all his thinking about human greatness and misery, about happiness, the heart and the wager, Pascal arrives at the centre of everything: Jesus Christ.

“Not only do we know God by Jesus Christ alone, but we know ourselves only by Jesus Christ. We know life and death only through Jesus Christ.”

Why? Remember the two mistakes from earlier: pride and despair. Pascal puts them side by side:

“The knowledge of God without that of man’s misery causes pride. The knowledge of man’s misery without that of God causes despair. The knowledge of Jesus Christ constitutes the middle course, because in Him we find both God and our misery.”

If you only know that God is great and good, but don’t see your own need, you get proud. You think you’re fine. If you only know how messed up you are, but don’t know God, you despair. You think there’s no hope.

Jesus shows us both at once. At the cross we see how serious our sin is, because it cost the Son of God his life. And we see how great God’s love is, because he gave it willingly. So Pascal says: “Jesus Christ is a God whom we approach without pride, and before whom we humble ourselves without despair.”

Pascal had another sharp saying about this: “There are only two kinds of men: the righteous who believe themselves sinners; the rest, sinners, who believe themselves righteous.” The people who are right with God are the ones who know they need him. The people who think they are fine on their own are the ones in trouble.

Pascal also thought hard about whether the story of Jesus is true. He spent many notes on the prophecies of the Old Testament and how Jesus fulfilled them. And he made a simple point about the first disciples: “The apostles were either deceived or deceivers.” They said they had seen Jesus risen from the dead. You can’t easily be mistaken about something like that. And if they were lying, why would they keep up the lie through prison, beatings and death? Pascal thought the best explanation was that they were telling the truth.

This is where all Pascal’s thoughts lead. The emptiness in us, the restlessness, the greatness and the misery, the heart’s longing, the wager, all of it points to one person. In Jesus, God is not a far-off idea or a frightening silence. He is someone you can know.

One thing to do this week: read Luke 24 this week, the story of the first Easter and Jesus appearing to his disciples. As you read, ask Pascal’s question: were they deceived, were they lying, or were they telling the truth? Then tell Jesus what you think.

study_questions.question: Why does knowing God without knowing our misery lead to pride?
study_questions.answer: Because we think we are fine and don’t see our need for him.

study_questions.question: How does Jesus show us both God and our misery?
study_questions.answer: At the cross we see how serious our sin is and how great God’s love is, so we can come to him without pride and without despair.

study_questions.question: What is Pascal’s argument about the apostles?
study_questions.answer: They were either deceived or deceivers; it is hard to be mistaken about a man risen from the dead, and liars would not have suffered and died for a lie.

fields.title: I Thought of You
fields.body_html:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.” — Matthew 26:38 (KJV)

Among Pascal’s notes is a short piece known as “The Mystery of Jesus”. It is not an argument. It is a prayer, written as Pascal thought about Jesus in the garden of Gethsemane on the night before he died.

Pascal describes Jesus in agony, praying alone while his closest friends fall asleep. He contrasts two gardens:

“Jesus is in a garden, not of delight as the first Adam, where he lost himself and the whole human race, but in one of agony, where He saved Himself and the whole human race.”

He notices that this is the one time Jesus asked for company and comfort from people, and they let him down. And then he writes a line that has stayed with readers ever since:

“Jesus will be in agony even to the end of the world. We must not sleep during that time.”

Pascal means that Jesus still suffers with his people everywhere, and we are called to stay awake, to pray, to care, and not to drift through life asleep to God and to other people’s pain.

Then something remarkable happens in the text. Pascal starts writing as if Jesus is speaking to him. These are the most personal words in the whole book:

“Console thyself, thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me.”

Think about what that means for a seeker. If you are looking for God, it is because God has already found you. Your longing for him is a sign that he is already at work in you. You did not start the search; he did.

“I thought of thee in Mine agony, I have sweated such drops of blood for thee.”

In the garden, facing the cross, Jesus was thinking of you. Not humanity in general. You. The drops of sweat and blood were for you.

Pascal kept his Memorial sewn into his coat until he died in 1662, aged only thirty-nine. In his last years he gave away much of what he had to the poor. He even moved out of his own house rather than turn out a poor family whose child had fallen ill. Among his last words was a prayer: “May God never abandon me.”

That is a good prayer to end with. Pascal, the genius, did not end his life with an argument. He ended it with trust in the God who had met him in fire, who had thought of him in Gethsemane, and who had promised never to leave.

One thing to do this week: read Matthew 26:36–46 slowly this week. Imagine yourself in the garden with Jesus. Then read Pascal’s line, “I thought of thee in Mine agony”, and thank Jesus for thinking of you there.

study_questions.question: What two gardens does Pascal contrast?
study_questions.answer: The garden of delight where Adam lost himself and the human race, and the garden of agony where Jesus saved the human race.

study_questions.question: What does “thou wouldst not seek Me, if thou hadst not found Me” mean for a seeker?
study_questions.answer: That the longing to seek God is itself a sign that God has already found us and is at work in us.

study_questions.question: How did Pascal live in his last years?
study_questions.answer: He gave much of what he had to the poor, and moved out of his own house rather than turn out a poor family whose child was ill.
